\paragraph{Decompression Mechanism.}
The spectral decompression phase reflects fine-tuning's redistribution of variance across embedding dimensions.
Pretrained Pythia-410M exhibits strong anisotropy ($\sigma_1{=}1943$, $r_{\text{eff}}{=}418$); early fine-tuning compresses this dominant direction ($\sigma_1$ drops 63\% by Gen~2) while inflating subordinate ones, resembling isotropy regularization~\citep{ethayarajh2019contextual} reversed by recursive amplification.
That downstream performance degrades during this expansion confirms these indicators are collapse detectors, not quality measures; their value lies in post-peak monotonicity.
SLV and perplexity are complementary: perplexity rises monotonically from Gen~0, making it a simpler monitor; SLV provides mechanistic diagnosis by distinguishing volume contraction from distributional broadening.

\paragraph{Prevention--Detectability Tradeoff.}
In ecology, stabilization interventions suppress the rising variance that serves as an EWS~\citep{scheffer2009ews}; our setting exhibits a stronger form: real-data mixing reverses the trajectory entirely.
Seven of eight indicators exhibit this reversal (\S\ref{subsec:alt_ews}), and the controller signal drops $10\times$ from $r{=}0$ to $r{=}0.2$ and vanishes at $r \geq 0.3$, leaving no regime where prevention and detection coexist.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
Our analysis reveals a reproducible three-phase collapse trajectory, identifies SLV as a cheap spectral indicator, and exposes signal attenuation that limits reactive controllers.
The trajectory map localizes $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$; setting $r > r_{\text{crit}}$ prevents collapse without per-generation monitoring, confirmed on GPT-2-medium, with preliminary evidence from Pythia-1B.

Synthetic data has become integral to language model training.
Instruction tuning, knowledge distillation, and data augmentation all routinely use model-generated text, and as synthetic corpora are recycled into training pipelines, the process often becomes recursive: each generation of models is fine-tuned on outputs from the previous one.
Recent work demonstrates that such recursive synthetic training triggers \textit{model collapse}, a progressive erosion of distributional tails and downstream capability~\citep{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024tails, alemohammad2024mad}.
The problem is especially pressing as web-scraped corpora increasingly contain model-generated content, a trend that introduces implicit recursive loops even without deliberate data reuse.

While model collapse is now well-characterized through theoretical analysis~\citep{dohmatob2024tails} and empirical studies~\citep{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024mad}, its effect on the geometric structure of learned representations remains poorly understood.
Characterizing how the embedding space contracts during recursive training could yield computationally cheap collapse indicators from internal model states alone, without text generation or benchmark evaluation.

Current collapse detection depends on downstream metrics such as perplexity and benchmark accuracy, or on analysis of generated text through lexical diversity measures.
Both approaches require either costly inference or external evaluation infrastructure at every generation.
SIGMA~\citep{gu2026sigma} introduced spectral monitoring through embedding covariance analysis and showed that spectral indicators can track collapse, but validated only on OPT-125M over short generation horizons.
Four gaps remain open.
First, no work has systematically characterized spectral dynamics beyond a few generations.
Second, the temporal relationship between spectral indicators and downstream degradation has not been examined.
Third, no study has connected spectral indicators to closed-loop collapse prevention through the lens of early warning signals (EWS)~\citep{scheffer2009ews}.
Fourth, the relationship between real-data mixing ratios and spectral collapse has not been mapped: it is unknown how much real data suffices to prevent spectral contraction, or whether a sharp phase boundary exists.

We address these gaps by tracking spectral indicators of the embedding matrix across 10 recursive generations of Pythia-410M-deduped~\citep{biderman2023pythia}, with pilot validation on Pythia-1B-deduped and cross-architecture confirmation on GPT-2-medium~\citep{radford2019language}.
Our analysis reveals a reproducible three-phase pattern (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}): spectral decompression (Gen~0--2), where effective rank ($r_{\text{eff}}$) and spectral log-volume (SLV) rise while downstream performance already declines; collapse onset (Gen~2--4), where spectral indicators reverse; and accelerating collapse (Gen~4--10), where contraction accelerates.
Among these indicators, SLV is the most effective collapse indicator: it requires only a forward pass on held-out data (no text generation), captures distributed volume changes across all spectral directions, and declines monotonically after its peak.
We further design a proportional controller as a testbed for reactive collapse prevention, and find that it exposes an inherent signal attenuation: the rate-based spectral signal degrades continuously as the real-data fraction increases and vanishes entirely above $r_{\text{crit}}$, rendering any reactive spectral controller ineffective in the regime where prevention succeeds.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{C1:} The first multi-seed spectral-downstream characterization over 10 recursive generations, revealing dynamics invisible in prior short-horizon studies and establishing a reproducible three-phase collapse pattern (decompression, onset, acceleration) across 10 generations (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}, Table~\ref{tab:phase0}).
\item \textbf{C2:} SLV as a computationally cheap collapse indicator with monotonic post-peak decline and a HellaSwag-spectral asymmetry: downstream degradation begins during the spectral decompression phase, demonstrating that spectral expansion does not indicate model health (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}).
\item \textbf{C3:} Quantitative characterization of signal attenuation under mixing: the spectral controller signal degrades continuously as the real-data fraction approaches $r_{\text{crit}}$ and vanishes entirely above it, a limitation robust to threshold reduction (\S\ref{subsec:controller}, \S\ref{subsec:phase1}).
\end{itemize}
Supporting these findings, we construct a spectral collapse trajectory map across multiple mixing ratios that localizes $r_{\text{crit}}$ empirically, with the bound robust to both the EMA smoothing parameter and random seed (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}, \S\ref{subsec:phase1}, \S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}), and provide preliminary cross-architecture evidence that the three-phase trajectory generalizes to GPT-2-medium (\S\ref{subsec:cross_arch}).

Synthetic data has become integral to language model training.
Instruction tuning, knowledge distillation, and data augmentation all routinely use model-generated text, and as synthetic corpora are recycled into training pipelines, the process often becomes recursive: each generation of models is fine-tuned on outputs from the previous one.
Recent work demonstrates that such recursive synthetic training triggers \textit{model collapse}, a progressive erosion of distributional tails and downstream capability~\citep{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024tails, alemohammad2024mad}.
The problem is especially pressing as web-scraped corpora increasingly contain model-generated content, a trend that introduces implicit recursive loops even without deliberate data reuse.

While model collapse is now well-characterized through theoretical analysis~\citep{dohmatob2024tails} and empirical studies~\citep{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024mad}, its effect on the geometric structure of learned representations remains poorly understood.
Characterizing how the embedding space contracts during recursive training could yield computationally cheap collapse indicators from internal model states alone, without text generation or benchmark evaluation.

Current collapse detection depends on downstream metrics such as perplexity and benchmark accuracy, or on analysis of generated text through lexical diversity measures.
Both approaches require either costly inference or external evaluation infrastructure at every generation.
SIGMA~\citep{gu2026sigma} introduced spectral monitoring through embedding covariance analysis and showed that spectral indicators can track collapse, but validated only on OPT-125M over short generation horizons.
Four gaps remain open.
First, no work has systematically characterized spectral dynamics beyond a few generations.
Second, the temporal relationship between spectral indicators and downstream degradation has not been examined.
Third, no study has connected spectral indicators to closed-loop collapse prevention through the lens of early warning signals (EWS)~\citep{scheffer2009ews}.
Fourth, the relationship between real-data mixing ratios and spectral collapse has not been mapped: it is unknown how much real data suffices to prevent spectral contraction, or whether a sharp phase boundary exists.

We address these gaps by tracking spectral indicators of the embedding matrix across 10 recursive generations of Pythia-410M-deduped~\citep{biderman2023pythia}, with pilot validation on Pythia-1B-deduped and cross-architecture confirmation on GPT-2-medium~\citep{radford2019language}.
Our analysis reveals a reproducible three-phase pattern (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}): spectral decompression (Gen~0--2), where effective rank ($r_{\text{eff}}$) and spectral log-volume (SLV) rise while downstream performance already declines; collapse onset (Gen~2--4), where spectral indicators reverse; and accelerating collapse (Gen~4--10), where contraction accelerates.
Among these indicators, SLV is the most effective collapse indicator: it requires only a forward pass on held-out data (no text generation), captures distributed volume changes across all spectral directions, and declines monotonically after its peak.
We further design a proportional controller as a testbed for reactive collapse prevention, and find that it exposes an inherent signal attenuation: the rate-based spectral signal degrades continuously as the real-data fraction increases and vanishes entirely above $r_{\text{crit}}$, rendering any reactive spectral controller ineffective in the regime where prevention succeeds.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{C1:} The first multi-seed spectral-downstream characterization over 10 recursive generations, revealing dynamics invisible in prior short-horizon studies and establishing a reproducible three-phase collapse pattern (decompression, onset, acceleration) across 10 generations (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}, Table~\ref{tab:phase0}).
\item \textbf{C2:} SLV as a computationally cheap collapse indicator with monotonic post-peak decline and a HellaSwag-spectral asymmetry: downstream degradation begins during the spectral decompression phase, demonstrating that spectral expansion does not indicate model health (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}).
\item \textbf{C3:} Quantitative characterization of signal attenuation under mixing: the spectral controller signal degrades continuously as the real-data fraction approaches $r_{\text{crit}}$ and vanishes entirely above it, a limitation robust to threshold reduction (\S\ref{subsec:controller}, \S\ref{subsec:phase1}).
\end{itemize}
Supporting these findings, we construct a spectral collapse trajectory map across multiple mixing ratios that localizes $r_{\text{crit}}$ empirically, with the bound robust to both the EMA smoothing parameter and random seed (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}, \S\ref{subsec:phase1}, \S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}), and provide preliminary cross-architecture evidence that the three-phase trajectory generalizes to GPT-2-medium (\S\ref{subsec:cross_arch}).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/spectral_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{SLV across 10 recursive generations of Pythia-410M (solid: $r{=}0$, 3-seed mean; dashed: $r{=}0.5$, 2-seed mean) under pure-synthetic training and 50\% real-data mixing. Three phases are visible in the pure-synthetic trajectory: decompression (Gen~0--2, SLV peaks at 2468), onset (Gen~2--4), and acceleration (Gen~4--10, SLV falls 11.6\% from peak to 2181). Under 50\% mixing, SLV rises monotonically (except a negligible Gen~1 dip) to 2572 at Gen~10, 8.7\% above baseline and 104 points above the pure-collapse peak.}
\label{fig:spectral_trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Decompression Mechanism.}
The spectral decompression phase reflects fine-tuning's redistribution of variance across embedding dimensions.
Pretrained Pythia-410M exhibits strong anisotropy ($\sigma_1{=}1943$, $r_{\text{eff}}{=}418$); early fine-tuning compresses this dominant direction ($\sigma_1$ drops 63\% by Gen~2) while inflating subordinate ones, resembling isotropy regularization~\citep{ethayarajh2019contextual} reversed by recursive amplification.
That downstream performance degrades during this expansion confirms these indicators are collapse detectors, not quality measures; their value lies in post-peak monotonicity.
SLV and perplexity are complementary: perplexity rises monotonically from Gen~0, making it a simpler monitor; SLV provides mechanistic diagnosis, as it distinguishes volume contraction from distributional broadening.

\paragraph{Prevention--Detectability Tradeoff.}
In ecology, stabilization interventions suppress the rising variance that serves as an EWS~\citep{scheffer2009ews}; our setting exhibits a stronger form: real-data mixing reverses the trajectory entirely.
Seven of eight indicators exhibit this reversal (\S\ref{subsec:alt_ews}), and the controller signal drops $10\times$ from $r{=}0$ to $r{=}0.2$ and vanishes at $r \geq 0.3$, leaving no regime where prevention and detection coexist.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
Our analysis reveals a reproducible three-phase collapse trajectory, identifies SLV as a cheap spectral indicator, and exposes signal attenuation that limits reactive controllers.
The trajectory map localizes $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$; setting $r > r_{\text{crit}}$ prevents collapse without per-generation monitoring, confirmed on GPT-2-medium, with preliminary evidence from Pythia-1B.

\paragraph{Model Collapse.}
\citet{shumailov2024collapse} showed that recursive training on model-generated data progressively erodes the tails of learned distributions, a phenomenon they termed \emph{model collapse}.
Scaling laws predict tail erosion as a function of recursive depth~\citep{dohmatob2024tails, dohmatob2024demystified, seddik2024synthetic}; the self-consuming loop accelerates collapse even under data accumulation~\citep{alemohammad2024mad}, with as little as 1\% synthetic contamination sufficing~\citep{dohmatob2025strong}, though preserving all prior real data can delay it~\citep{gerstgrasser2024inevitable}; alternative strategies include self-verification filtering of synthetic outputs~\citep{fu2025selfverification} and leveraging weak non-synthetic data~\citep{amin2025escaping}.
We complement these output/benchmark-based diagnoses by tracking collapse through the spectral geometry of internal representations, requiring no text generation.
Unlike neural collapse~\citep{papyan2020prevalence}, which describes last-layer features converging to a simplex ETF in classification, spectral collapse in recursive training reflects progressive embedding volume loss unrelated to class structure.

\paragraph{Spectral Analysis of Representations.}
Random matrix theory reveals implicit regularization structure in neural network eigenspectra~\citep{martin2021implicit}; effective rank~\citep{roy2007effectiverank} and RankMe~\citep{rankme2023} quantify representational dimensionality.
The spectral decompression phase, in which singular value spread decreases while effective rank increases, resembles the effect of isotropy regularization~\citep{ethayarajh2019contextual}; recursive fine-tuning may initially reduce the anisotropy documented in standard training~\citep{gao2019representation} before amplifying it during collapse.
Recent work has connected spectral properties to training pathologies: \citet{he2025spectral} linked spectral collapse in hidden representations to plasticity loss in continual learning, and \citet{naderi2025mindgap} identified spectral rank collapse in attention matrices as a failure mode of deep transformers.
Most directly relevant, \citet{gu2026sigma} proposed SIGMA, a spectral monitoring framework that tracks singular-value distributions during recursive training on OPT-125M over three generations.
Mathematically, our SLV is equivalent to half of SIGMA's $\log\det G$ (both sum log singular values of the embedding matrix), establishing a shared metric foundation.
When $n < d$, both metrics face the same rank-deficiency issue; our $\epsilon$-thresholding (\S\ref{subsec:spectral_metrics}) makes the equivalence approximate rather than exact.
Our work extends SIGMA in \emph{scale} (Pythia-410M/1B, 3--8$\times$ larger), \emph{temporal depth} (10 generations vs.\ 3, enabling the discovery of the three-phase trajectory, signal attenuation, and the collapse trajectory map, all invisible at SIGMA's horizon), and \emph{methodology} (closed-loop SLV-based mixing control; \S\ref{subsec:controller}).
At three generations spectral indicators are still rising (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}), which could lead to the premature conclusion that spectral health implies model health.
Finally, \emph{signal attenuation}, whereby successful mixing suppresses spectral indicators that would have warned of collapse, is a phenomenon that short-horizon monitoring does not encounter.

Early warning signals (EWS) for critical transitions originate in ecology, where rising autocorrelation and variance precede regime shifts~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}, with detection methods ranging from statistical tests~\citep{dakos2012methods} to deep learning~\citep{bury2021deeplearning}.
A central tension is that stabilization interventions suppress the very precursors they rely on~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}.
Rate-induced critical transitions~\citep{siteur2016ecosystems} further demonstrate that interventions can themselves alter system dynamics.
We encounter a parallel tension: real-data mixing reverses the spectral trajectory entirely (\S\ref{subsec:controller}), unlike ecological stabilization which preserves signal direction; our contribution is quantifying how rapidly this signal degrades across mixing ratios.
\citet{he2025spectral} provides a bridge between these domains by connecting spectral collapse to critical transitions in continual learning.

\paragraph{Data Mixing for LLM Training.}
Data composition significantly affects LM quality~\citep{longpre2024pretrainer, muennighoff2023scaling}, and several methods optimize domain mixtures through proxy models or predictive formulas~\citep{xie2023doremi, ye2025mixinglaws, chen2025aioli}.

Our work reveals a complementary dimension: real-vs-synthetic mixing reshapes the spectral geometry of internal representations, producing a trajectory map (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}) that loss-based metrics do not capture, and our controller targets recursive spectral collapse rather than general domain balance.

\paragraph{Decompression Mechanism.}
The spectral decompression phase reflects fine-tuning's redistribution of variance across embedding dimensions.
Pretrained Pythia-410M exhibits strong anisotropy ($\sigma_1{=}1943$, $r_{\text{eff}}{=}418$); early fine-tuning compresses this dominant direction ($\sigma_1$ drops 63\% by Gen~2) while inflating subordinate ones, resembling isotropy regularization~\citep{ethayarajh2019contextual} reversed by recursive amplification.
That downstream performance degrades during this expansion confirms these indicators are collapse detectors, not quality measures; their value lies in post-peak monotonicity.
SLV and perplexity are complementary: perplexity rises monotonically from Gen~0, making it a simpler monitor; SLV provides mechanistic diagnosis, as it distinguishes volume contraction from distributional broadening.

\paragraph{Prevention--Detectability Tradeoff.}
In ecology, stabilization interventions suppress the rising variance that serves as an EWS~\citep{scheffer2009ews}; our setting exhibits a stronger form: real-data mixing reverses the trajectory entirely.
Seven of eight indicators exhibit this reversal (\S\ref{subsec:alt_ews}), and the controller signal drops $10\times$ from $r{=}0$ to $r{=}0.2$ and vanishes at $r \geq 0.3$, leaving no regime where prevention and detection coexist.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
Our analysis reveals a reproducible three-phase collapse trajectory, identifies SLV as a cheap spectral indicator, and exposes signal attenuation that limits reactive controllers.
The trajectory map localizes $r_{\text{crit}} \in (0.25, 0.3]$; setting $r > r_{\text{crit}}$ prevents collapse without per-generation monitoring, confirmed on GPT-2-medium, with preliminary evidence from Pythia-1B.

\subsection{Cross-Architecture Validation}
\label{subsec:cross_arch}

To test whether the three-phase trajectory generalizes beyond Pythia, we repeat the recursive pipeline on GPT-2-medium~\citep{radford2019language} (355M parameters, different pretraining corpus and tokenizer) under four conditions: pure synthetic ($r{=}0$, 9 generations), intermediate mixing ($r{=}0.25$ and $r{=}0.3$, 3 generations each), and a real-data control ($r{=}1.0$, 3 generations).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}clrrrl@{}}
\toprule
$r$ & Type & SLV$_0$ & SLV$_{\text{end}}$ & $\Delta$SLV & Pythia? \\
\midrule
0    & I    & 689  & 415\,(G9)  & $-$39.8\% & \checkmark \\
0.25 & ---  & 689  & 738\,(G3)  & $+$7.0\%  & $\dagger$ \\
0.30 & III  & 689  & 737\,(G3)  & $+$6.9\%  & \checkmark \\
1.0  & Ctrl & 689  & 813\,(G3)  & $+$17.9\% & \checkmark \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (355M, seed~42). \textbf{Pythia?}: whether the trajectory type matches the corresponding Pythia-410M classification. $\dagger$\,Three-generation horizon does not resolve the Type~II/III distinction at this ratio.}
\label{tab:cross_arch}
\end{table}

Under pure synthetic training, GPT-2-medium reproduces the three-phase pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch}): SLV peaks at Gen~2 (924, $+$34.1\% from baseline) and declines to 415 by Gen~9 ($-$55.1\% from peak), while perplexity rises from 15.5 to 329 ($+$2028\%).
The $\sigma_1$ trajectory follows the same U-shape (6598$\to$1191 during decompression, rising to 1593 by Gen~9), confirming that dominant-direction reconcentration under falling effective rank is architecture-independent.
The collapse magnitude is substantially larger than Pythia's ($-$55.1\% vs.\ $-$11.6\% SLV decline), reflecting GPT-2-medium's more anisotropic initial spectrum ($r_{\text{eff}}{=}23$ vs.\ Pythia's 418).

The real-data control ($r{=}1.0$) shows monotonic expansion with perplexity \emph{decreasing} ($-$27.4\%), which confirms that collapse is specific to recursive synthetic training.

At intermediate ratios ($r{=}0.25$, $r{=}0.3$), both conditions reproduce the decompression phase (Gen~0$\to$1: SLV $+$8.5\%, $r_{\text{eff}}$ from 23 to 142, $\sigma_1$ $-$82\%) and stabilize through Gen~3, with EMA-smoothed SLV monotonically non-decreasing.
At $r{=}0.3$ this matches Pythia's Type~III classification.
At $r{=}0.25$, the three-generation window does not resolve the Type~II/III distinction, since Pythia's characteristic EMA dip appears only at Gen~5+; the trajectory is consistent with the Pythia-410M phase boundary but does not independently confirm $r_{\text{crit}}$ for this architecture.
